extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of literature, and critics interested in the craft of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the literary craft and evaluative standards for composing and judging novels: character design, plot/story, narrative voice, pattern, prose rhythm, fantasy/prophecy, and moral effect. Focuses on what makes a novel artistically successful rather than on publishing mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story vs. Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes a 'story' (a simple chronological sequence of events) from a 'plot' (a sequence of causally related events that produces a distinct emotional/ethical effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forster's illustrative contrast: 'The King died, and then the Queen died' (story) versus 'The King died, and then the Queen died of grief' (plot). Aim for plot when you want artistic shape and emotional force; story suffices for mere reporting of incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: People (real life) vs. Characters (fictional constructs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separates 'people' as complex realities and 'characters' as literary constructs used to create effects in fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist may either imitate 'people' or deliberately create 'characters' with a controlling idea. Be conscious whether you intend lifelike complexity or an emblematic/constructed figure; both are legitimate but must be handled knowingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat versus Round Characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are built around a single idea or quality and remain essentially the same; round characters are complex and capable of surprising the reader 'in the way that people surprise us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Famous Forster formulation: round characters are 'capable of surprising in a convincing way.' Use flat characters where a consistent, repeatable function is needed (comic types, plot engines); cultivate roundness when psychological depth and development matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs. Telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiates 'showing' (presenting scenes and sensory detail so readers perceive events) from 'telling' (narratorial summary, explanation, or commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing for dramatic and character moments; employ telling for necessary compression, transitions, or when the narrator's voice must comment. Balance is important: not everything can or should be dramatized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as Causal and Necessary Arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot requires arranging incidents so that each follows causally or meaningfully from what precedes; episodes should not be gratuitous but contribute to the pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When building plot, ensure events are motivated and that their order produces the intended emotional or intellectual effect. Avoid mere succession of exciting incidents without causal or thematic connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy and the Fantastic Element
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of fantasy or supernatural material in the novel: such elements are permissible but must obey the internal logic of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy can amplify truth and meaning, but the author must maintain consistency of the fantastic element's rules. Distinguish types (fairy-tale, allegory, pure fantasy) and choose the tone and boundaries accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy vs. Art (Didacticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the novelist-as-prophet (preaching or moralizing) and the novelist-as-artist whose moral effects arise from the work itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware overt sermonizing; moral or prophetic statements are stronger when they emerge organically from characters and events. The artist should prioritize imaginative truth over explicit didacticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern, Unity, and Architectural Shape
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel should have an underlying pattern or shape—an architecture that unifies incidents, motifs, and emotional curves into a coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan or discover patterns (recurrence, symmetry, contrast) that give the novel cohesion. Chapters, episodes, and motifs should contribute to the overall design rather than be loose or merely episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and Cadence of Prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose rhythm—the musical quality produced by sentence length, punctuation, and arrangement—is a crucial aesthetic element of the novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence and paragraph lengths to create momentum, repose, or emphasis. Attend to the sound and flow of language; spacing of clauses and choice of words affect the reader's emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Prose Style (Diction and Tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must be appropriate to subject, period, and characters; clarity, simplicity, and aptness are virtues while purple, pretentious, or ill-fitting diction harms the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match voice to material; avoid unnecessary ornament. Let prose serve the novel's aims—tell, suggest, evoke—rather than call attention to itself unless rhetorical effects are intentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle of Vision / Point of View
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of narrative perspective—omniscient, limited, central consciousness, etc.—shapes what is revealed and how readers empathize with characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and maintain a consistent angle of vision appropriate to the material. A limited or central consciousness can create intimacy; omniscience allows breadth and authorial commentary. Inconsistency in viewpoint undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Effect (Implicit Ethics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ethical or moral dimension of a novel should arise from its characters' lives and situations rather than from direct moralizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for moral complexity: show consequences, allow ambiguity, and let readers infer moral lessons. Heavy-handed morals weaken artistic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability, Verisimilitude, and Convincing Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when events are improbable, they must be made convincing within the fictional world; surprises should feel believable for the characters involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground improbable incidents in credible motives, antecedents, or thematic logic so that readers accept them. A 'surprising' action is good only if it is consistent with character and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic Devices and Irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of comedy, comic characters, and ironic distance as legitimate aspects of the novel; irony can illuminate character and theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance comic elements with seriousness; use irony to reveal truth without merely mocking. Comic types may be deliberately flat; irony should cohere with the novel's overall purpose.
